Anatomy · Forbidden Planet, MGM 1956

Robby the Robot

How the machine works, twice over. MGM built him in 1955 as a three-piece suit with a stuntman inside and a cable running out of his heel. On screen he is Dr. Morbius's servant on Altair IV, with a chemical laboratory in his belly and an inhibition that no order can override. This page draws both, and tags every claim by where it comes from.

System by system 09 assemblies

Numbered as in the figure's parts list. Each assembly says what the film shows, how MGM actually built it, and how it might work if it were real. Only the last kind is our invention, and it is always marked.

01Clear shell, ears and radar mast

Prop MGM's construction sheet calls it the clear plastic dome16, but it is not a dome. The head is a bullet 17.34 in across and about 21 in tall on ArthMat's dimensioned drawing, standing on a brim cut on a slant: 4.45 in above the chest at the back and 7.19 in at the front15. The Plexiglas covers the whole upper part of that bullet. Below the ears it runs on down the front only, as a window over the keys, between the cheeks of a black hood that makes the sides and back15,17. Seen past the glare in photographs, the clear part is a cap with a tongue hanging down the front.

Prop The model shop's schedule gave the plastic dome three weeks, 15 February to 8 March 19557. When Fred Barton first saw the prop in 1973 it had yellowed6.

1954 script Robby turns his whole dome through 180 degrees to face his passengers, and a small radar antenna has come up out of Robby's dome, and is slowly rotating when he scans for Altaira2.

Film He reports Something is approaching from the southwest. It is now quite close. The monster arrives minutes later1.

Speculative Altair IV's air is high in oxygen, and Robby says it promotes rust1. A sealed shell keeps the key chassis and gyros out of it. The mast in the figure rises 22 cm through a gland at the apex, so the radar can sweep without the head turning. Take the figure apart and the clear shell lifts off whole, so its shape can be read on its own.

02Gyro tower and pilot lamp

Prop MGM's sheet labels the top of the head revolving gadgets16. Inside the glass: a pilot light at the very top, three white wire-frame spheres that orbit in planetary fashion to represent gyroscopic stabilizers, and a pair of reciprocating arms in an inverted V3. Barton's replica, moulded from the original, mounts the gyros on a spun brass bell under a heat sink and lamp housing5. The mechanisms were loud when powered up3.

1954 script Robby calls his built-in reflexes infallible and drives Morbius's car fast enough that the Doc begs him to keep it under ninety2.

Speculative A seven-foot walker on small, stiff steps needs a balance reference. Read as working parts, the three gyros are rate sensors on one carrier, and the figure spins them faster whenever Robby is computing: when he composes speech, analyses a sample, or fights an order.

03Head: voice tubes and key chassis

Prop Behind the window the hood is flat and black, with vent slots, a strip of small indicator bulbs, a row of keys on coil springs and a red lamp at each end. Above the hood the same black chassis carries the gyro tower on its top deck, inside the clear cap15,17. Comb fins stand out from each cheek between the brim and the ears15.

Prop The mouth is a collar of parallel thin blue neon tubes, MGM's voice tubes16, that light in step with his speech. The same grille let the operator see out and breathe3. On set an off-camera actor spoke into a microphone, and a voice-actuated circuit ran through a cable into Robby's foot, up a leg, to the neon. Marvin Miller re-recorded the voice afterwards3.

Prop The ears are two rotating chrome rings, MGM's rotating rings16, one on a horizontal shaft and one on a post. The CAD drawing tilts that post 30 degrees15. The eyes are two small blinking lights on cones, and across the front sits a row of levers like saxophone keys3. On the drawings and replicas the cones are the ear hubs on the hood's cheeks, so the eyes look forward from either side of the window. The left hub's whiskers stand up in a V; the right hub's point outward15,17. On Barton's replica six relays strike in turn, three times each, just before Robby speaks5.

1954 script Asked how he drives without looking, Robby answers I do everything by positronic transfiguration, and winks several lights to prove it2.

Speculative Two scanners on crossed axes sweep a whole sphere between them, which is why one turns horizontally and one vertically. The six keys read as the output stage of a speech composer: they strike, then the neon carries the words.

04Chest barrel and indicator panel

Film Morbius demonstrates: One introduces a sample of human food through this aperture. Down here there's a small built-in chemical laboratory where he analyzes it. Later Robby reproduces the molecules in any shape or quantity1.

1954 script The aperture is jaw-like, and reproduction happens right in his own workshop2.

Prop The barrel shape is a nod to Kinoshita's earlier work designing washing machines. Below the sample door sit two rotating discs with flashing lights and a row of five buttons that move in and out3. Barton calls this the heart box: an oscillating acrylic star, a brass quad light that turns, and pulsating piano keys5. MGM's sheet names the whole box the analyzing hopper & indicator panel16. It is 10.74 in wide on the CAD drawing, standing proud of a barrel 16.5 in tall15.

Prop Wikipedia counts five buttons3. The CAD drawing, MGM's sheet and the replicas we followed all show four, and so does the figure15,16,17.

Speculative In the figure the door drops like a jaw into a small tray, the throat behind it feeds the analyzer drum in the core, and the keys stand out further while the lab is working.

05Laboratory core

Speculative Nothing inside Robby's chest is shown on screen, so this assembly is invented, built only from what the dialogue implies. The abdomen holds an analyzer; manufacture comes later and elsewhere. The core in the figure has an analyzer drum on two cradles, a throat up to the sample door, a pattern store, a reflex pack, and the relay cage for his inhibitions. Every part fits through the barrel's 41 cm floor opening, so the chest can lift off without touching it.

1954 script When Altaira overrides him at the door she says Emergency cancellation Limberlock. Clear relays D-12,000 to D-18,500. That is 6,501 relays, the only numbered hardware anyone ever names inside him2. The cage's top rail carries the range as its one engraved label.

06Arms and claws

Prop MGM's sheet calls each shoulder a flexible sleeve & ball socket, draws the arm in locked position, and specifies a tool adaptor & tools16. On the CAD drawing the sockets sit in drums of radius 6.50 in at the barrel's front corners15.

Prop Thick, stubby arms on plastic ball joints with limited rotation. They can extend under an expanding concertina sheath of rubber, and end in three-fingered rubber hands painted gunmetal grey3. The Bonhams lot included alternate claw hands4.

Film Tremendously strong, of course. He could quite easily topple this house off its foundation. He carries ten tons of isotope 217 on his vehicle, and the wounded Doc is the only person he ever carries1,3.

1954 script Morbius asks for a Stillson wrench, and Robby detaches his own left hand and fits the wrench in its place. Spare parts, one of them a metal hand, ride clipped to his body2.

Speculative Swappable tools imply a standard wrist coupling, which MGM's tool adaptor makes explicit; it is drawn here as the collar between sleeve and palm. The arms leave their sockets along the drum's axis when the figure comes apart.

07Pelvis and hip hinges

Prop The lower section hinges at the top of the legs, so the suit can bend forward and swing slightly, and the globes hide the operator's hips and knees3. The weight of all three sections hung from a flying harness on the actor's shoulders, and a special frame let him rest between takes10.

1954 script At the car Robby goes round in front, sits down, engaging his rear end in the drive mechanism2. He plugs into his vehicle.

Speculative The hip pivots in the figure double as that drive coupling: the same joint that lets him bend would carry torque into the car.

08Legs and feet

Prop Interlocking vacuum-formed plastic globes with internal joints. Walking was possible in small, stiff steps3, on completely flat floors only. Frankie Darro, who stood 5 ft 3 in, was replaced by Frankie Carpenter after a near tumble10,3. Inside, the robot was built around aluminium tracks, and it walked almost silently apart from a creak of plastic6.

Prop MGM's sheet marks the leg length this dimension to fit operator, and asks for an alternate sole with ball bearing casters for pulling sequence16. That second sole let Robby be towed on wheels in shots where he could not walk.

Film Sorry, miss, I was giving myself an oil job.1

Speculative The figure's proportions come from ArthMat's CAD drawing in inches, which totals about 84 in, the prop's 7 ft. Legs and pelvis stand 42.24 in (107 cm) to the chest. Each leg is three squat globes of radius 6.00, 5.60 and 6.00 in on an oval shoe 15.71 in long and 11.17 in wide15. Next come a pelvis 58 cm across, a barrel 74 cm across and 42 cm tall, the voice collar, and the shell, 44 cm across and 52 cm tall.

09Riser, gauge and console

Prop Power came through a cable out of Robby's heel, or from onboard batteries10, run from a remote control panel on wheels11. Bonhams sold that auxiliary control panel with him and lists it at 17 × 23.75 × 39 in. The console in the figure is drawn at that size, with the off-camera microphone mounted on it11,4.

Speculative The riser, turntable dais and height gauge are display furniture. The gauge's rider sits at 214 cm, and the cable runs from the console's gland to a connector on the right shoe.

The inhibition how an order fails

Robby's one hard rule is never stated as a law. It is shown three times, and each time it beats a direct order.

  1. Order

    Morbius hands Robby the commander's blaster and has him fire at a shrub on the terrace. Robby: A simple blaster.

  2. Check

    Then: point it at the commander, between the eyes, fire. The target is a rational being.

  3. Lock

    Robby freezes, locked in a sub-electronic dilemma between my direct orders and his basic inhibitions against harming rational beings.

  4. Cancel

    Morbius cancels the order. If I were to allow that to continue, he would blow every circuit in his body.

At the door, after dark

Film I am monitored to admit no one at this hour. My beams are focused on your blasters, gentlemen. The Doc asks whether he has a built-in rule against wringing their necks: That is true, sir. Yet I am monitored to admit no one.1

1954 script In the script their blasters fail, and Robby warns he cannot prevent you gentlemen from damaging yourselves against me2.

Film Altaira releases him: Robby, emergency cancellation Archimedes.1

1954 script The 1954 script spells the same override out as hardware: Emergency cancellation Limberlock. Clear relays D-12,000 to D-18,500.2

The last order

Film With the monster tearing through the steel shutters, Morbius orders Kill it, Robby. Robby does nothing. Adams: He knows it's your other self.1

1954 script The Robot stands motionless. His gadget lights have gone out.2

Speculative The refusal is the film's proof. A machine that cannot harm a rational being will not fire on the monster, so the monster must be part of a man: Morbius himself. Wikipedia compares the rule to Asimov's Three Laws3; the 1957 sequel shows what happens when a computer removes it9.

The build and after 1954–2017

  1. Aug–Sep 1954

    1954 script Cyril Hume's shooting script already describes a robot with no face, only a complicated arrangement of electronic gadgets.2

  2. 1954–55

    Prop Concepts from A. Arnold Gillespie, Arthur Lonergan and Irving Block are refined by illustrator Mentor Huebner. Robert Kinoshita builds a miniature about 10 in tall; the art director takes it to the producer and comes back with Draw it!3,7

  3. 15 Feb–8 Mar 1955

    Prop The MGM model shop's schedule for building Robby; three weeks go to the plastic dome. Parts are early ABS (Royalite), vacuum-formed over wooden moulds.7,3

  4. 1956

    Film Forbidden Planet opens. Frankie Darro and Frankie Carpenter wear the suit; Marvin Miller's voice is dubbed in; Bebe and Louis Barron's circuits supply the film's electronic tonalities.3,13

  5. 1957

    Film The Invisible Boy gives Robby a new origin: brought back by time machine from a Chicago spaceport of 2309, then rebuilt by a boy under the influence of a supercomputer, which strips his prohibition against harming people.9

  6. 1958–1984

    Prop Decades of reuse on television and film: The Gale Storm Show, The Twilight Zone (a toy in 1959; an oil-can head in Uncle Simon), Lost in Space, Columbo, Project U.F.O. with a one-eyed head, Mork & Mindy, and a cameo in Gremlins.3

  7. 1970–71

    Prop MGM sells him to Jim Brucker's Movie World / Cars of the Stars museum in Buena Park, where he is often vandalised. Sources disagree on the year.3,10

  8. 1973–74

    Prop Fred Barton finds him painted silver, missing an ear, a scanner, the blasters and the heart-box detail, legs warped, ankles broken, dome yellowed, yet the neon tubes and every MGM mechanism functioned. Barton strips, moulds and restores him in about two months.6

  9. 1979–80

    Prop Director William Malone buys Robby, his car, spare parts and shipping cases. Sources disagree on the year.3,10

  10. 2004

    Prop Inducted into the Robot Hall of Fame.3

  11. 21 Nov 2017

    Prop Bonhams New York sells suit, car, control panel, alternate claws, the Uncle Simon head and crates for $5,375,000, then the highest price for a film prop at auction.4,12,11

How the figure was made

Proportions come from ArthMat's dimensioned CAD drawing, in inches, scaled to Wikipedia's 214 cm15,3. Part names come from MGM's construction sheet16. Photographs of replicas and renders of the clear shell settled what the drawings leave open, chiefly where the clear plastic stops. It covers the cap of the bullet head and runs down the front as a window. A black hood makes the cheeks and back, carries the ears and comb fins, and shows through the window as a dark recess behind the keys17. The console follows Bonhams' dimensions. Every turned body (shoes, globes, pelvis, barrel, collar, brim, head) is an analytic profile, and every part records its true shape, so a geometry audit can check that nothing passes through anything at rest, apart, or at any moment in between. The laboratory core and the readings marked Speculative are ours. Drawn with the Anatomy skill's kit.14
